soil-class-130.q: Where does the name Kastanozem come from?
soil-class-130.a: From the Russian and Latin words for chestnut, after the colour of the chestnut's husk.

soil-class-140.q: Why are most Retisols left under forest or pasture?
soil-class-140.a: Water drains through their clay-poor tongues while the dense clay parts are often too dry and hard to root, and earthworms avoid them.

soil-class-124.q: What does the high magnetic susceptibility of chernozem suggest about how it formed?
soil-class-124.a: Heat turns goethite and ferrihydrite into maghemite, so it points to fire, likely set by early humans.

soil-class-074.q: Why does draining a peatland release carbon dioxide?
soil-class-074.a: Drainage exposes organic carbon, built up underwater over thousands of years, to the air, where it decomposes to CO2.

soil-class-053.q: Why does terra preta resist leaching when the soils around it do not?
soil-class-053.a: Its charcoal stays in the soil for thousands of years, binding minerals and nutrients.

soil-class-078.q: Which kind of peat is the least decomposed: fibric, hemic or sapric?
soil-class-078.a: Fibric peat, which consists of intact fibre; sapric peat is the most decomposed.

soil-class-051.q: Why is terra rossa popular for growing wine?
soil-class-051.a: The karstic rock beneath gives it high internal drainage, surprisingly good for a clay-rich soil.

soil-class-081.q: How does tropical peat differ in origin from the temperate kind?
soil-class-081.a: It forms mostly from dead trees rather than the sphagnum typical of temperate peat.

soil-class-049.q: Why do brown podzolic soils lack the continuous E horizon of a true podzol?
soil-class-049.a: Soil creeping downslope keeps supplying iron and aluminium oxides, which build up as an orange-brown B horizon.

soil-class-067.a: A shallow depression of heavy clay floods after seasonal rains, and as the water evaporates a dried, fissured crust forms on the surface.

soil-class-052.q: Why does a latosol lose its fertility once the rainforest above it is felled?
soil-class-052.a: Its fertility lies in a thin humus layer fed by the forest; once that is no longer replaced, the nutrients leach away quickly.

soil-fert-181.a: An organism needs it for normal function but cannot make it itself, at all or in sufficient amounts.

soil-fert-169.q: Which plant nutrients do not come originally from the soil's mineral fraction?
soil-fert-169.a: Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, supplied by carbon dioxide and water, and nitrogen, supplied by nitrogen fixation.

soil-fert-153.q: What did Albert Howard call the basis of the public health system of the future?
soil-fert-153.a: Soil fertility; he wrote that all future studies of disease must begin with the soil.

soil-fert-150.q: Why do inorganic fertilizers act at once?
soil-fert-150.a: Plants take up nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in inorganic forms, which these fertilizers supply directly.

soil-fert-197.q: Why do legumes short of molybdenum fix less nitrogen?
soil-fert-197.a: Molybdenum is needed for nitrogenase, the enzyme of nitrogen fixation.

soil-fert-157.q: How do root hairs free cations held on soil particles?
soil-fert-157.a: They pump hydrogen ions into the soil, which displace cations held on negatively charged particles.

soil-fert-188.q: What does liming a garden soil to pH 6.5 do about lead?

soil-fert-159.q: Is iron part of the chlorophyll molecule?
soil-fert-159.a: No, but it is essential for making chlorophyll.

soil-fert-161.q: How can heavy phosphate applications cause zinc deficiency?

soil-fert-180.q: Why can cobalt matter to legumes though it seems inessential for most plants?
soil-fert-180.a: It is essential for nitrogen fixation by bacteria associated with legumes.

soil-fert-194.q: Why is nitrogen usually the hardest nutrient to manage?
soil-fert-194.a: Plant-available nitrogen changes quickly with soil water.
